questions.text: Step 7 says the new image can't be ready without store keys, and step 3 writes the keys first. But old pods use the old yaml keys. When the new pods start using the new keys, what happens to the old pods' keys at the provider: do both keep working at the same time until step 10?
What is the 'managed secret store' here, and how does a pod prove who it is to it? What does 'the pod's identity (orders-api-prod)' mean in practice?
Step 15 says the client reads the key from memory on every call. In step 14, when the refresh swaps the key, how does the 'previous value kept for one generation' get used and when is it dropped?
In step 7, how does a rollout 'hold after the first new pod'? Is this a manual pause by a person, and who decides to continue?
questions.about: Step 7 Merge, then roll out to prod

questions.text: Step 7 says old pods are only stopped once the new pod is ready. Does a new pod's readiness depend on anything other than loading the three keys, like a successful call to the providers?
Who is 'the security on-call' and how do they find the provider's 'last used' time for the old key in step 10? Is that something every provider shows?
What does the 'alert' in step 14 look like and where does it fire from? How does the app or monitoring know that no refresh succeeded for 15 minutes?
In step 8, the check says the pod's logs show the expected version id. How are the expected version ids known, and what does 'post-migration image' mean concretely (a tag, a digest)?
questions.about: Step 8 Confirm every instance is on the new keys

answers.text: Yes. Old and new keys are both valid at the provider from step 3 until step 10. Old pods use the yaml keys and new pods use the store keys at the same time. This was already in the Approach; I added it to step 7 context by stating it at the top of the Approach.

The brief only says 'our managed secret store' and gives no product or auth mechanism. The pod's identity is the cluster service identity orders-api-prod from deploy.md, which the platform attaches to the pod, so no credential sits in the image or env. The exact proof mechanism (for example workload identity) is not known; I added it to Assumptions.

On each swap the old value becomes 'previous', replacing whatever was previous before, so only one older value is held. It is used only by the step 15 fallback when the provider rejects the current key. It is dropped at the next swap. Clarified in step 14.

Yes, a manual pause by whoever runs the deploy. They run the per-provider smoke call, check the error rate, and decide to continue. Reason: it catches a bad new key before all pods use it. Clarified in step 7.

No. Readiness depends only on holding all three keys. No provider call is made, so a provider outage cannot block a rollout. The provider smoke check is a separate manual check at the step 7 hold. Added to step 12.

The security on-call is the group given write on prod secrets in step 1. Where each provider exposes 'last used' (dashboard or API) is not known, and not every provider may show it. I added that to step 2 as something to confirm, to the step 10 gate, and to Assumptions, with a fallback of disable-first and a day of watching errors.

The pod logs secret_refresh_ok on each successful refresh, and the central log service alerts when a pod has none for 15 minutes. This is simplest because logs already exist. Whether the log service supports this alert is not verified, so it is in Assumptions. The alert is my addition, not in the brief.

Expected version ids are the ones the store returned in step 3, recorded in the ticket (and updated if a key is rewritten). The post-migration image is identified by its digest, recorded in the ticket at step 7, not a tag. Both are now stated in steps 3, 7 and 8.

questions.text: Step 3 says the old keys stay active, but step 10 revokes them 'one provider at a time'. Between step 3 and 7, who or what stops the old pods from restarting or scaling and picking up something unexpected? Do old pods ever read the store?
Step 5 says clients fetch the key from the secrets module on every call. Is that module reading process memory only, or does it call the store each time? Where does the in-memory value get set?
questions.about: Step 5 Code change / Step 13 Holding secrets in memory

questions.text: In step 12, what does 'latest version' mean for a secret that was rewritten in step 3 (version 2 after a correction)? Does the app ever pin to a specific version id?
questions.about: Step 12 Startup load / Step 3 If it fails

questions.text: In step 7, how is it decided that the first new pod is bad and the rollout must be stopped or rolled back? What does the deploy person look at to judge the 'error rate'?
questions.about: Step 7 Merge, then roll out to prod

questions.text: Step 8 says no refresh line shows an older version afterwards. What would cause a pod to log an older version, since the store only returns the latest?
questions.about: Step 8 Confirm every instance is on the new keys

questions.text: In step 15, how does the client know a 401/403 is caused by a bad key and not something else, and what happens to the customer request while the re-read and retry occur?
questions.about: Step 15 If the provider rejects the key

questions.text: Step 9 says old image tags contain the leaked keys. Why is that an issue if the keys are revoked in step 10, and who enforces 'do-not-deploy' in the deploy tooling?
questions.about: Step 9 Bake, then block the old images

answers.text: Old pods run the old image with yaml keys and never read the store, so a restart or extra old pod behaves exactly as before. The old keys stay valid until step 10. Stated in the Approach.

The secrets module returns the key from process memory only; it does not call the store per request. Memory is set by the startup load (step 12) and the 5-minute refresh (step 14). Reason: no store latency or outage on the request path. Stated in steps 5 and 13.

'Latest' means the newest version the store holds at read time, so a corrected rewrite (version 2) is used automatically. The app never pins a version id, which keeps rotation restart-free. Stated in step 12.

The plan now gives a concrete rule: continue only if the per-provider read-only calls succeed and the new pod's logs show no 401 or 403. Which dashboard or metric the team uses for a broader provider error rate is not known, so I dropped the vague 'error rate' wording. The smoke calls are in Assumptions.

Normally nothing: the store returns the latest, so a pod showing an older version is stuck, failing to refresh, or did not restart. The check is simplified to: the latest log line per secret shows the expected id. The 'no older line afterwards' clause was removed. Step 8.

The client cannot tell, so on any 401 or 403 it re-reads and retries once; if the key was not the cause the retry fails too and the original failure is returned. The customer request waits for at most one re-read and one retry, each within its timeout. Safe because auth rejections are not processed. Step 15.

The real problem is rollback: after step 10 an old image would run with revoked keys and fail every provider call. The leaked keys are dead by then, so that reason is secondary. Which tool enforces do-not-deploy (registry delete or deploy tooling policy) is not known; it is now in Assumptions.

teachbacks.text:
1. Trigger: the plan is approved. Two things start in parallel. Step 1 builds the store layout: paths `orders-api/prod/*` and `orders-api/dev/*`, each environment with its own KMS key, and an access policy kept as infrastructure code in review. `orders-api-prod` can read prod secrets and decrypt with the prod key and has no write access. Only the security on-call group can write prod. Engineers cannot read prod but can read dev. The step is done when three tests pass: an engineer is denied a prod read, `orders-api-prod` is denied any write, and `orders-api-prod` is denied reads on dev and on other apps' paths. If it fails, nothing consumes it yet, so fix the policy and re-run. Step 2 inventories every consumer of the current keys (the 4 prod pods, non-prod deployments, laptops running `make run`, CI jobs, other services). It also checks that each provider (payments, email, geocoding) allows two active keys at once, and whether it shows a "last used" time. The results go in the migration ticket. If a provider allows only one key, stop and escalate for that provider. Any consumer found late would break when the old key is revoked.

2. Step 3 starts when steps 1 and 2 are done. The security on-call creates a new key at each provider while the old keys stay active. They write each new key directly into `orders-api/prod/<name>`, where the names are `payments_api_key`, `email_api_key` and `geocoding_api_key`. The value never passes through chat, tickets, CI variables, shell history or environment variables. The store, which encrypts with KMS, returns a version id per write. The ids go in the ticket and are used later as the expected ids. They also check each new key with one read-only authenticated call. State is held at the provider (old and new keys both valid) and in the store (version 1 of each secret). A failed write is retried. A wrong value is overwritten, which makes a new version id, and the ticket is updated. An exposed new key is revoked and replaced.

3. Step 4 sets up dev. It starts after step 1 and must finish before the code merges. Sandbox or test keys go in `orders-api/dev/*`. `make run` sets `APP_ENV=dev` and reads that path using the engineer's own identity, through the same code path as prod. `make run-offline` sets `APP_ENV=local` and uses an in-process fake secret source with dummy values and stub provider URLs. The fake source refuses to start unless `APP_ENV=local`. If a provider has no sandbox, dev uses stubs for it and never a live key.

4. Step 5 is the code change, which starts after steps 1 and 4 and can run in parallel with step 3. The three `api_key` lines are removed from `config/app.yaml`. A new secrets module keeps the keys in process memory. Only its startup load and refresh talk to the store. The clients in `app/clients/*` no longer copy the key at init. On every call they ask the module for the current key, which is a memory read. Importing `config_loader` no longer needs secrets. `/healthz` returns 200 only after the startup load succeeds. The tests, using a fake store and log capture, are: startup makes 4 attempts then exits non-zero; readiness is withheld until all three keys are loaded; a failed refresh keeps the last good value and logs a warning; no key value appears in logs, environment or temp directory.

5. Step 6 is the CI guard, and it must ship in the same PR as step 5. A CI job parses `config/app.yaml` as YAML and fails if any mapping key named `api_key` appears at any depth, or if the file doesn't parse. It is a required status check on `main`. It has a negative-test fixture and a throwaway PR that re-adds a key and must be blocked.

6. Step 7 is merge and rollout. It starts when steps 3, 4, 5 and 6 are done and the review is complete. Merging must not happen before step 3 finishes, because the merge builds an image that cannot become ready without the store keys. The new image rolls out one pod at a time with `maxUnavailable: 0`. Part B describes what each new pod does at startup:
   a. The process starts. The app fetches the latest version of each of the three secrets from `orders-api/<APP_ENV>/<name>`, never pinning a version. It authenticates as the pod's service identity (`orders-api-prod`), which the platform provides. Each fetch has a timeout.
   b. If the store is unreachable or a secret is missing, it retries 3 times, 2 seconds apart, for 4 attempts in total. After the fourth failure it logs an error naming the secret and exits with code 1. Kubernetes restarts the pod.
   c. The values are held in process memory. Each key sits in an object that is swapped whole and redacts itself when printed. Keys never go into environment variables, disk or logs. Only version ids are logged, as `secret_loaded name=… version=…`.
   d. `/healthz` returns 503 until all three keys are held, then 200. It makes no provider call.
   e. When a new pod is ready, an old pod is stopped. If the new pod never becomes ready, the rollout halts and the old pods keep serving with the old, still valid keys. Old pods run the old image unchanged and never read the store.
   f. After the first new pod is ready, the deployer pauses the rollout by hand. They make one authenticated read-only call per provider through that pod and check the logs for 401 or 403. They continue only if all three calls succeed and there are no 401 or 403 lines. Otherwise they stop and roll back, which means redeploying the earlier image. This still works until step 10. The new image digest is recorded in the ticket.

7. In normal operation, a request to a provider works as follows (step 15). The client reads the current key from memory and sends it. If the provider answers 401 or 403, the client cannot tell whether the key is the cause, so it always tries the fallback. It does one out-of-cycle re-read of that secret, at most once a minute per secret. If the version changed, it retries once with the new value. Otherwise it retries once with the "previous" value, if one is held. If neither works, it returns the original failure. This is safe because an auth rejection means the provider did not process the request. The document marks this as the author's own addition to be confirmed.

8. Refresh (step 14): a timer fires every 5 minutes after startup. For each secret the app fetches the latest version. If the version id differs, it swaps in the new value, keeps the old one as "previous" (only the one value before the current one), and logs `secret_rotated name=… old_version=… new_version=…`. If the version is the same, it logs `secret_refresh_ok`. If a re-read fails, the app keeps the last good value, logs a warning with the secret name and error class, and tries again at the next tick. Readiness is never changed by a failed refresh. An alert fires if a pod logs no `secret_refresh_ok` for 15 minutes.

9. Step 8 confirms every instance is on the new keys, once the rollout has finished. For each of the 4 pods, listed from the cluster at check time, two things must hold. The pod runs the digest recorded in step 7. For each secret, the latest `secret_loaded` or `secret_rotated` log line shows the version id recorded in step 3. Non-prod deployments and other consumers from step 2 are checked too. If any instance can't be shown to be on the new key, step 10 does not start. Investigate it, and restart it if that is the only fix.

10. Step 9 is the bake period, which starts when step 8 passes and lasts as long as the team chooses (at least one business day is suggested). Pre-migration image tags are marked do-not-deploy or deleted, because after step 10 they would fail every provider call and still contain the leaked keys. Developers are told to use the new `make run`. If a rollback is needed during the bake, roll back to the old image, repeat steps 7 to 9 later, and re-run the step 8 check before any revocation.

11. Step 10 revokes the old keys. The security on-call decides, after re-running the step 8 check before each revocation. The order is geocoding, then email, then payments. The gate for each key is that the provider's "last used" for the old key has stopped advancing for at least 15 minutes. If the old key is still being used, find the consumer first. If the provider has no "last used", use the disable-first method and watch its error rate for a day. Where supported, disable the key first and delete after a day with no errors. If errors appear after a disable, re-enable the old key and find the consumer. A hard delete cannot be undone.

12. Step 11 closes out once all three old keys are revoked. Update `deploy.md` and the runbook, record the final version ids, and confirm the CI guard is required on `main`. Git history is not rewritten. The ticket stays open until the guard and the do-not-deploy marks are verified.

13. Later rotations (step 16) repeat steps 3, 8 and 10. The security on-call writes a new key to the store. Within 5 minutes every instance swaps through the refresh, and the version ids in the logs confirm it. Then the old key is revoked. No restart or redeploy is needed. The document leaves open whether keys must also be rotated on a schedule.
gaps: How a pod proves its identity to the store is not specified. The document says only that the platform gives the pod a service identity and that the mechanism depends on the store.
The document does not say what the read-only authenticated smoke calls are for each provider (steps 3 and 7).
Step 8 compares the version ids to those recorded in step 3. The document does not say how the expected id is handled if a corrected rewrite in step 3 made a new id, beyond updating the ticket.
The document does not say how the person running the deploy reads the pod logs or gets the pod to make the provider calls in the step 7 check.
